result: Temperature-sensitive mutant experiments demonstrate that Sh1-associated germ cells differentiate before DTC-associated germ cells. In emb-30(ts) animals at restrictive temperature, germ cells under Sh1 differentiate while those under the DTC remain undifferentiated, with the transition zone shifting to align with the Sh1 boundary. Similarly, in glp-1(bn18) animals at restrictive temperature, germ cells under Sh1 enter meiosis first while DTC-associated cells remain stem-like.
evaluation: Claims C4, C5, C26-C32, C36-C42 collectively provide strong experimental evidence from two independent temperature-sensitive mutant systems (emb-30 and glp-1) with appropriate controls. The data in Figure 1 shows statistically significant results with proper replication (Figure 1—figure supplement 1). The Sh1 position remains constant while the differentiation boundary shifts to align with it, supporting the conclusion that Sh1 marks a functional boundary between stem-like and differentiating germ cells.

result: Endogenously tagged membrane proteins (mKate::INX-8, GFP::INX-9, ina-1::mNG, cam-1::mNG) consistently mark the distal Sh1 boundary at <40 µm from the distal end, coinciding with the stem cell niche exit zone. These markers provide reliable visualization of Sh1 without measurably impairing gonad function.
evaluation: Claims C6, C45-C49, C105-C106 are supported by consistent observations across multiple independent endogenously tagged proteins (Figure 2A-D). The concordance among different molecular markers acting in distinct pathways strengthens the conclusion. The position measurements are quantitative and align with prior work on stem cell zone boundaries (C48 with citation to Lee et al., 2019).

result: Overexpressed transgenic markers (lim-7p::ced-1::GFP, lim-7p::GFP, lim-7p::GFP::CAAX) show high variability in localization and frequently fail to label the distal Sh1 boundary. The lim-7p::ced-1::GFP marker is particularly unreliable, with only low-expressing animals (<400 AU) consistently showing a DTC-Sh1 interface.
evaluation: Claims C7, C50-C55, C82, C84 are well-supported by quantitative fluorescence intensity analysis (Figure 3A) and comparison with endogenous markers. The correlation between expression level and detection of distal Sh1 (C54: 100% interface detection at low expression vs. 50% overall) provides strong evidence for incomplete labeling at high expression levels. The conclusion that lim-7p::ced-1::GFP is an unacceptable marker (C84) is justified by the data.

result: The lim-7p::ced-1::GFP transgene causes incompletely penetrant gonad morphology defects (~20% penetrance) in both DG5020 and DG5131 strains, including gonad migration failures and abnormal membrane protrusions. These defects are not observed in strains with endogenously tagged proteins alone.
evaluation: Claims C8, C74-C77, C81, C83 are supported by quantitative observations (Figure 4A-C) showing similar defect rates in two independent strain backgrounds. The absence of such defects in qy78-only strains (C76) strengthens the conclusion that the transgene is responsible. The morphological defects are well-documented with images (Figure 4A, B, E).

result: The two Sh1 cells of a pair can have dramatically different distal positions, with one cell often extending 20+ µm farther distal than the other. This asymmetry is revealed by variable transgene expression and confirmed by co-expression of CED-1::GFP with mKate::INX-8, where 6/15 morphologically normal gonads showed discrepancies between the two markers.
evaluation: Claims C9, C10, C57-C58, C60, C62, C64-C68 are supported by detailed imaging analysis (Figure 3B-F, Figure 3—figure supplement 1). The quantitative data (23/31 cases showing >20 µm difference, C68) and cross-sectional analysis (Figure 3E) provide strong evidence. This is a novel finding that was previously unknown (C60), making it particularly significant.

result: A synthetic interaction exists between lim-7p::ced-1::GFP and inx-8(qy78), evidenced by 50% reduction in mKate::INX-8 signal in regions with high CED-1::GFP expression and by enhanced gonad defects in the double-marked strain DG5131 compared to either marker alone.
evaluation: Claims C70-C73, C93 are supported by quantitative fluorescence measurements (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E-F) and phenotypic analysis (Figure 5). The 50% reduction in INX-8 signal (C71) is quantified with background subtraction. The synthetic interaction is further supported by the dramatically shortened proliferative zone in DG5131 (79 µm) compared to DG5020 (91 µm) or NK2571 (106 µm), with statistical significance demonstrated (Figure 5D).

result: The NK2571 strain with endogenously tagged inx-8(qy78) has normal distal gonad patterning indistinguishable from wild-type (106 µm vs. 109 µm proliferative zone, 5.1 vs. 4.6 dividing cells, 639 µm vs. 670 µm gonad length). In contrast, DG5131 combining qy78 with lim-7p::ced-1::GFP shows significant defects in all three measures (79 µm proliferative zone, 3.2 dividing cells, 575 µm gonad length).
evaluation: Claims C88-C103 are supported by comprehensive quantitative analysis with appropriate statistical testing (Figure 5B-E). The comparison across four strains (N2, NK2571, DG5020, DG5131) with multiple metrics provides strong evidence. Statistical significance is properly assessed with one-way ANOVA and Tukey's post-hoc tests, with detailed results in figure legends. The conclusion that qy78 alone does not cause defects (C103) while the combination does (C102) is well-supported.

result: All fluorescently marked strains show mildly to moderately reduced brood sizes compared to wild-type.
evaluation: Claim C87 is supported by brood size data in Table 1, showing reductions ranging from 12% (cam-1::mNG) to 37% (DG5131). However, the authors appropriately note that brood size is an emergent property of many processes and not a direct measure of distal gonad function. The data are presented with appropriate sample sizes and error estimates.

result: INX-8 and INX-9 expression differentiates in the adult, with INX-8 signal diminishing from the DTC while INX-9 signal persists.
evaluation: Claims C43-C44 are supported by imaging data (Figure 1D showing white DTC outline with INX-9 but not INX-8). This is a straightforward observational result with clear visual evidence.

result: In DG5131 animals, CED-1::GFP intensity is notably low, and lower expression levels appear more likely to reveal the distal Sh1 cell, possibly because high levels are not tolerated in distal Sh1.
evaluation: Claims C78-C79 are supported by quantitative fluorescence data (Figure 4D). However, C80 is explicitly speculative (marked as SPECULATION in evidence_type), presenting alternative explanations without definitive evidence. The overall result is supported but includes acknowledged uncertainty about mechanism.

result: The N-terminal mKate::INX-8 and GFP::INX-9 tags are most likely extracellular based on innexin-6 channel structure determined by cryo-EM.
evaluation: Claim C69 is supported by inference from cited structural data (Oshima et al., 2016). This is a reasonable inference based on homology to a structurally characterized innexin, though it is not directly demonstrated for INX-8 or INX-9.

result: Variable expression levels and complete silencing of C. elegans transgenes are well-known phenomena.
evaluation: Claim C59 is established knowledge supported by citation (Evans, 2006). This provides context for interpreting transgene variability observed in the study.

result: Background knowledge claims about C. elegans germline anatomy, Notch signaling, temperature-sensitive mutants, and innexin genetics.
evaluation: Claims C1-C2, C14, C16-C20, C23-C25, C33-C35, C85-C86, C112 represent established knowledge supported by citations to prior literature. These provide necessary context for the experimental work but are not novel findings of this study.

result: Prior findings from Gordon et al., 2020 and other recent work establishing the distal position of Sh1 and its association with germ cells exiting the niche.
evaluation: Claims C3, C11-C13, C15, C21-C22, C107-C111 represent findings from prior work, primarily Gordon et al., 2020, that provide the foundation for the current study. These are appropriately cited and provide context for the confirmatory experiments presented here.

result: Speculative explanations for observations, including possible reasons for CED-1::GFP localization failures and Sh1 cell position differences.
evaluation: Claims C56 and C113 are explicitly speculative (marked as INFERENCE or SPECULATION in evidence_type), presenting possible explanations without definitive evidence. These represent reasonable hypotheses but are not experimentally tested in the current work.

result: A major role of inx-8/9 is in the proximal gonad regulating the provisioning of oocytes with essential metabolites.
evaluation: Claim C104 is a hypothesis from another study (Tolkin et al., 2022) that the authors find compelling but is not directly tested in this work. It is marked as SPECULATION and CITATION in evidence_type. While it may explain some observations (like high embryonic lethality in inx-9(qy79)), it is not a finding of the current study.

result: The existence of an interface between the DTC and Sh1 cells that coincides with the boundary of the distal-most stem-like germ cells is supported by the preponderance of evidence.
evaluation: Claim C114 represents the overall conclusion of the study, synthesizing evidence from multiple experimental approaches (temperature-sensitive mutants, multiple endogenous markers, analysis of transgene variability). The conclusion is appropriately cautious ('preponderance of evidence') while being well-supported by the totality of data presented. This is the central thesis confirmed by the study.
